introduction: "Every knowledge hath seventy meanings." These passages teach that the words of God have meanings without end, outer and inner and the inner of the inner; that some verses are clear and others are figures; that prophecies and stories in the Bible and the Qur’an are often to be read symbolically; and that there is also an authorized interpreter whose word settles disputes. They include many worked examples. Ninety-seven outside voices stand beside them: the Talmud's hammer on the rock, Paul's allegory and veil, Origen, Augustine, Aquinas and Maimonides, the verses and stories being interpreted, and Spinoza and Newton; with Humpty Dumpty, Montaigne, Blake and Shakespeare to ask what stops a reader from finding whatever he likes.
questions: If the meanings of a verse are infinite, what makes one reading better than another? Compare Augustine's "why not both, if both be true?" with Humpty Dumpty.
The Báb says that whoever accepts the outward without the inward, or the inward without the outward, has not believed. How does that differ from Paul's "the letter killeth"?
Several passages restrict authoritative interpretation to one person. What does that leave for the individual reader, and what does it protect?
Take one worked example from the guide (Methuselah's years, the sons of God, the bread of heaven) and compare the verse in its own words with the reading given.
‘Abdu’l-Bahá says that the history in the Torah was written by Ezra, as Spinoza had argued. How does that fit with reverence for the book?
A talk asks where Jesus speaks of the wrath of God. How do the Gospels and Paul answer, and how should hard sayings be read?

outside.why: The Talmud says that as a hammer breaks a stone into many fragments, so one verse spoken by God yields several explanations.
Jesus told his disciples that he had many things to say which they could not bear yet.
Daniel was told that the words were closed up and sealed until the time of the end.
Augustine, hearing two readers each claim Moses for his own meaning, asks: why not rather both, if both be true?
A psalm makes the sparrow that nests at the altar a figure for the soul that longs for God.
Aquinas held that since the author of scripture is God, it is not unfitting for one word to bear several senses.
Isaiah speaks of a vision that has become like a sealed book, which neither the learned nor the unlearned can read.
This is the verse of the Qur’an on clear and ambiguous verses, whose interpretation none knows save God.
Humpty Dumpty says that a word means just what he chooses it to mean. If divine words have infinite interpretations, what keeps a reader from doing the same?
The second letter of Peter says that Paul's letters contain things hard to understand, which the unstable twist.
Shakespeare's Antonio remarks that the devil can cite scripture for his purpose. Is clinging to the clear verses a protection against that?
This is the verse quoted: thy Lord shall come with angels, rank on rank.
Bacon warned that the understanding is no dry light, but is coloured by what a person wishes to be true.
Paul sets love above prophecy and knowledge, which are partial and pass away.
The Buddha said that he had taught with no closed fist and no distinction of inner and outer doctrine.
Emerson, quoting an older saying, held that every scripture is to be interpreted by the same spirit that gave it forth.
The second letter of Peter says that no prophecy of scripture is of private interpretation.
Blake says to his opponent: we both read the Bible day and night, but thou readest black where I read white. What follows if no two minds comprehend alike?
Philip asks a traveller reading Isaiah whether he understands, and the man replies: how can I, unless someone guides me?
Plato's Socrates says that written words cannot answer a question and always need their author's help. What is an authorized interpreter for?
The Talmud holds that a verse never departs from its plain meaning, whatever else it also teaches.
Paul says that the letter kills and the spirit gives life. The Báb holds that outward and inward conform and neither may be denied. How do the two rules differ?
Origen argued that some things in scripture cannot be meant literally and were placed there to send the reader inward.
Paul reads the story of Abraham's two sons as an allegory of two covenants.
Shelley says that all high poetry is infinite: veil after veil may be drawn aside, and the inmost meaning never laid bare.
Jeremiah hears that the word is like a fire, and like a hammer that breaks the rock in pieces.
Montaigne complained that there is more ado to interpret interpretations than to interpret things. Does endless meaning enrich a text, or bury it?
Proverbs says that understanding is found by those who search for it as for hidden treasure.
This is the verse to which the letter alludes: if the sea were ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would be spent first.
John's Gospel ends by saying that the world could not contain the books that might be written.
The Revelation of John has God name himself by two letters, the first and the last.
A psalmist calls his tongue the pen of a ready writer, moved by what his heart is composing.
Jesus says that he speaks in parables because his hearers see without seeing.
Jesus tells his disciples that to them it is given to know the mysteries of the kingdom.
Paul says that the things of the Spirit are spiritually discerned, and are foolishness to the natural man.
The Tao Te Ching says that the name that can be named is not the enduring name.
The Qur’an says that to God belong the most beautiful names, by whichever he is called.
Daniel blesses the God who reveals the deep and secret things and knows what is in the darkness.
John sees a city, the new Jerusalem, that is also a bride: an image that already asks to be interpreted.
Paul says that the things which are seen are temporal, and the things not seen are eternal.
The Qur’an names God the First and the Last, the Outward and the Inward.
This is the verse quoted: if all the trees were pens and the sea ink, the words of God would not be exhausted.
Paul speaks of the deep things of God, which the Spirit searches and reveals.
The Qur’an's verse of light is itself a parable within a parable: a niche, a lamp, a glass, a star.
Jesus thanks God that these things are hidden from the wise and revealed to whom he wills.
This is where the Qur’an tells of Abraham and the star, with the moon and the sun in the verses that follow.
This is the passage of the Revelation, which itself calls the seven stars a mystery and gives a meaning.
John was told to seal up what the seven thunders said and not to write it.
Jesus tells a Samaritan woman that worship belongs neither to this mountain nor to Jerusalem, but to spirit and truth.
Maimonides also taught that the wolf dwelling with the lamb is a figure, and that the world will follow its ordinary course.
Luke says that the risen Jesus expounded in all the scriptures the things concerning himself.
This is the verse asked about, in which Mary's people address her as sister of Aaron.
This is the verse of Genesis asked about, on the sons of God and the daughters of men.
This is the opening of Genesis, with the Spirit of God moving on the face of the waters.
Joseph says to the prisoners who have dreamed: do not interpretations belong to God?
Genesis tells of Joseph's dream of sheaves, which his brothers understood at once.
This is the verse quoted, on the living brought forth from the dead.
Moses saw a bush that burned with fire and was not consumed.
The Qur’an itself uses a tree as a likeness: a good word is as a good tree, its root firm and its branches in heaven.
This is the saying of Jesus that the talk explains, comparing himself to the serpent Moses lifted up.
Mill held that whoever knows only his own side of a case knows little even of that.
This is the saying of Jesus about other sheep that are not of this fold.
Jesus says: love your enemies, and pray for those who persecute you. How are the denunciations of the older prophets to be read beside that?
Paul writes that the wrath of God is revealed against all ungodliness. How does this talk's reading of the New Testament deal with such sentences?
Jesus himself calls some of his hearers a generation of vipers. Is there a severity in the Gospels that the question here passes over?
A psalm says that the Lord is merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and will not keep his anger for ever.
Jesus refuses to give a sign to those who ask for one.
Hume would accept a miracle only on testimony whose falsehood would be more miraculous. Does treating miracles as of no importance answer him or agree with him?
The rabbis had a rule for this: the Torah speaks in the language of men.
This is the verse that gives Methuselah nine hundred and sixty-nine years.
The second letter of Peter says that with the Lord one day is as a thousand years.
A psalm says that a thousand years in God's sight are as yesterday when it is past.
These are the verses, at the end of the books of Moses, that tell of his death and burial.
Spinoza drew the same conclusion from the same evidence in 1670: the Pentateuch as we have it was not written by Moses.
Nehemiah tells how Ezra and the Levites read in the book of the law and gave the sense.
Paul's rule is: prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
This is the saying in John's Gospel: I am the bread of life.
Paul says that a veil lies on the heart when the old scriptures are read, and is taken away in turning to the Lord.
Luke says that Jesus opened his disciples' understanding so that they might understand the scriptures.
Paul says that those who condemned Jesus fulfilled the very prophets that were read to them every sabbath.
This is the promise in John's Gospel of another Comforter, who will abide for ever.
Jesus charged the teachers of his day with making the word of God void through their tradition.
This is the verse quoted on abrogation: nothing is abrogated or forgotten but a better or the like is brought.
Paul says that he fed his hearers with milk and not with meat, because they were not yet able to bear it.
Newton held that prophecy was given not to make interpreters into prophets, but to be understood when it is fulfilled.
The Qur’an says that they would put out the light of God, and that God will perfect his light.
The people of Berea searched the scriptures daily to see whether what they had been told was so.
A psalm prays: open thou mine eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of thy law.
At Pentecost people from every nation heard the same message, each in his own language.
Jesus says: search the scriptures, for they are they which testify of me.
Mark says that Jesus spoke in parables as his hearers were able to hear, and explained them in private.
Aristotle held that the greatest thing by far is to have a command of metaphor.
Plato teaches by an image, the cave, how images lead toward what is real.
Shakespeare's duke finds books in the running brooks and sermons in stones.
Thomas Browne read two books, scripture and nature, the public manuscript that lies open to all.
At the burning bush the name given is: I AM THAT I AM.
Blake asks to see a world in a grain of sand, and eternity in an hour.

john-bread-of-life.text: And Jesus said unto them, I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger; and he that believeth on me shall never thirst

john-as-moses-lifted-up.text: And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up: That whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have eternal life

genesis-sons-of-god.text: And it came to pass, when men began to multiply on the face of the earth, and daughters were born unto them, That the sons of God saw the daughters of men that they were fair; and they took them wives of all which they chose

genesis-spirit-moved-upon-the-waters.text: In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth. And the earth was without form, and void; and darkness was upon the face of the deep. And the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters

deuteronomy-moses-died.text: So Moses the servant of the Lord died there in the land of Moab, according to the word of the Lord. And he buried him in a valley in the land of Moab, over against Bethpeor: but no man knoweth of his sepulchre unto this day

revelation-seven-stars.text: The mystery of the seven stars which thou sawest in my right hand, and the seven golden candlesticks. The seven stars are the angels of the seven churches

genesis-interpretations-belong-to-god.text: And they said unto him, We have dreamed a dream, and there is no interpreter of it. And Joseph said unto them, Do not interpretations belong to God? tell me them, I pray you

jeremiah-hammer-that-breaketh-the-rock.text: Is not my word like as a fire? saith the Lord; and like a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces

psalm-slow-to-anger.text: The Lord is merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and plenteous in mercy. He will not always chide: neither will he keep his anger for ever

quran-sister-of-aaron.text: O sister of Aaron! Thy father was not a wicked man nor was thy mother a harlot.

talmud-hammer-breaks-a-stone.text: Just as this hammer breaks a stone into several fragments, so too, one verse is stated by God and from it emerge several explanations

shelley-veil-after-veil.text: All high poetry is infinite; it is as the first acorn, which contained all oaks potentially. Veil after veil may be undrawn, and the inmost naked beauty of the meaning never exposed
shelley-veil-after-veil.author: Percy Bysshe Shelley

montaigne-interpret-interpretations.text: There is more ado to interpret interpretations than to interpret things
montaigne-interpret-interpretations.author: Michel de Montaigne

emerson-interpreted-by-the-same-spirit.text: Every scripture is to be interpreted by the same spirit which gave it forth
emerson-interpreted-by-the-same-spirit.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

augustine-why-not-rather-as-both.text: when one shall say, He meant as I do, and another, Nay, but as I do, I suppose that I am speaking more religiously when I say, Why not rather as both, if both be true
augustine-why-not-rather-as-both.author: Augustine of Hippo

carroll-just-what-i-choose-it-to-mean.text: it means just what I choose it to mean
carroll-just-what-i-choose-it-to-mean.author: Lewis Carroll

aquinas-several-senses.text: Since the literal sense is that which the author intends, and since the author of Holy Writ is God, Who by one act comprehends all things by His intellect, it is not unfitting, as Augustine says (Confess. xii), if, even according to the literal sense, one word in Holy Writ should have several senses
aquinas-several-senses.author: Thomas Aquinas
aquinas-several-senses.translator: Fathers of the English Dominican Province
